title: Opinion: The haze returns. So where are the independent directors? - The Edge Malaysia
text:
Opinion: The haze returns. So where are the independent directors? Wednesday 04 Nov 2026 BURSA SGX Home 
 Opinion Make The Edge Malaysia your preferred source on Google Every year, the haze returns. Air quality deteriorates, schools and businesses adjust their operations, and millions across Southeast Asia bear the economic and social costs of a problem that has persisted for decades. The debate usually focuses on who started the fires. Was it a plantation company, a contractor, a supplier or a smallholder? Yet after years of recurring haze, perhaps we should be asking a different question: who was responsible for ensuring the fires never started in the first place?
 The annual haze is no longer merely an environmental issue. It is also a corporate governance issue. Unlike a cyberattack or an unexpected economic shock, haze is a foreseeable risk. Boards understand seasonal weather patterns, historical fire hotspots, regulatory expectations and the reputational damage that can result from environmental incidents. If corporate governance exists to identify and manage foreseeable risks, then recurring haze raises an uncomfortable question: why do such failures continue to occur despite decades of governance reforms, sustainability commitments and ESG reporting?
 At the centre of this discussion sits the independent director. Independent directors are expected to provide objective oversight, challenge management where necessary and protect the interests of shareholders and stakeholders alike. They are often described as guardians of good governance and serve as an important counterbalance to executive power. Yet the recurring haze invites a broader question: do independent directors possess sufficient authority, accountability and professional standing to perform that role effectively?
 Many independent directors are nominated through processes influenced by existing boards, major shareholders or management. Their remuneration is paid by the companies they oversee, while their reappointment frequently depends on the same organisations they may need to challenge. This does not undermine their integrity. Rather, it highlights a structural weakness within the governance system. When significant environmental or governance failures occur, attention is naturally directed towards management. However, independent directors also have an oversight responsibility. Were difficult questions asked? Were warning signs escalated? Were management assurances rigorously challenged? Or were directors informed only after problems had emerged?
 Good governance should not be judged solely by how organisations explain failures. It should also be judged by how effectively foreseeable risks are prevented. This is particularly relevant in an era of increasingly sophisticated ESG reporting. Companies disclose climate risks, sustainability commitments and responsible sourcing policies in impressive detail. Yet disclosure is not accountability. A company can publish an excellent sustainability report while governance weaknesses remain unresolved. Committees can meet regularly, dashboards can be reviewed and policies can be updated, while underlying risks continue to grow. The haze reminds us that governance is ultimately measured by outcomes, not disclosures.
 If recurring haze represents a governance failure, then perhaps it is time to rethink the institution of independent directorship itself. The discussion should move beyond training alone. Many independent directors already attend seminars, conferences and professional development programmes. The question is not whether learning opportunities exist but whether attendance alone is sufficient assurance of competency.
 We do not ask whether a surgeon attended a seminar before entering an operating theatre. We ask whether the surgeon remains professionally competent to carry out the responsibilities entrusted to them. Perhaps it is time to ask the same question of independent directors.
 Accountants, auditors, lawyers and engineers operate within recognised professional frameworks. They are subject to accreditation standards, professional codes of conduct, continuing competency requirements and disciplinary processes when standards are breached. Yet independent directors oversee organisations worth billions of ringgit, influence thousands of employees and make decisions with significant financial, environmental and social consequences. Despite this, independent directorship remains closer to an appointment than a profession.
 That should change.
 Malaysia already has a strong foundation through the Institute of Corporate Directors Malaysia (ICDM), which has played an important role in director development. The next step should be to elevate independent directorship into a recognised profession. Public-listed companies should ordinarily appoint independent directors from a recognised pool of professionally accredited directors. Where a board chooses to appoint an individual who does not possess such accreditation, it should be required to explain to shareholders why that individual possesses equivalent governance competencies. In other words, the principle should be simple: comply or explain.
 Such an approach would not exclude former regulators, business leaders, academics or professionals from serving on boards. Rather, it would establish a common benchmark of governance competence while preserving flexibility. A national register of accredited independent directors could strengthen confidence in board oversight and raise professional standards across the market.
 Accreditation, however, should involve far more than attending courses. It should include competency assessments, periodic recertification, adherence to a professional code of conduct and continuous evaluation against emerging governance challenges such as sustainability oversight, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and supply chain risks. Most importantly, accreditation should be accompanied by accountability. Independent directors are not responsible for day-to-day management, but they should be accountable for exercising effective oversight. Just as auditors sign audit opinions, independent directors could periodically attest to the adequacy of board oversight over material risks facing the organisation. A signature carries responsibility, and responsibility influences behaviour.
 The annual return of haze should concern more than environmental regulators and public health authorities. It should also prompt reflection in boardrooms.
 For years, Southeast Asia has debated who lit the fires. Perhaps the more important question is whether we have given independent directors the authority, professionalism and accountability necessary to help prevent them. If the answer is no, then strengthening the independent director profession is not a future governance agenda but an overdue reform whose time has already arrived.
 And the haze may be reminding us of that fact, year after year.
 Francis Xaviour Joe is client relations director at Sustainlaterre PLT, a sustainability-related software solutions provider.
